one_liner: A direction to nudge a decision rule to pick better actions more often.
everyday: Imagine you are a robot learning to pick fruit from a tree. Right now, your rule is: when you see a red fruit in the upper left, reach up 60 degrees. You try it and get a good piece of fruit—that was a smart decision. But your rule also has some random noise in it, so sometimes you reach up 58 degrees or 62 degrees by accident. How do you teach yourself to repeat the good move? You cannot just retrace your steps exactly; you need to know which parts of your decision-making process to strengthen. Policy gradient solves this: it tells you the direction to change your decision rule so that the actions you took become more likely in the future, weighted by how good those actions turned out.

In reinforcement learning, your decision rule is called a policy. The policy is a set of rules that looks at the current situation and decides what to do. Policy gradient works like this: you act in the world, you see a reward (good or bad), and then you compute a gradient—a direction of change. This direction points toward making your policy more likely to do things that led to high rewards and less likely to do things that led to low rewards. The gradient tells you how to tweak each part of your decision-making process, and the amount you tweak is weighted by the advantage—how much better that action was compared to average—so that high-reward actions pull the policy much harder than low-reward ones. If an action gave you twice the normal reward, you increase its probability twice as much because the advantage is twice as large.

This method works without knowing the true reward function or having an explicit plan. You only need to: take actions, see what happens, measure the advantage, and then nudge your policy in the direction that makes good actions more likely. It applies equally to simple rules and to deep neural networks—anything that can compute a gradient can be improved by this approach. The formula treats the gradient of your policy's logarithm as the direction to move, and multiplies it by the advantage to scale the step size.
symbols: The policy gradient—the direction to change your policy to increase expected reward.
The expected value—the average across many episodes or samples.
The gradient of the logarithm of your policy's probability. It points in the direction that makes an action more likely.
The advantage—how much better this action was compared to the average. Positive means better, negative means worse.
Multiplication of the gradient direction by the advantage weighting factor.

worked.title: A simple decision with two possible actions
lines: Policy π says: action A has probability 0.3, action B has probability 0.7.
log π(A) = log(0.3) ≈ -1.2; gradient ∇log π(A) ≈ 3.33 (points in direction to increase this probability).
You took action A and got advantage A = 2.0 (it was 2 units better than average).
You increase the weights (the numbers inside the policy model) that led to action A with step size 6.66.
Action A's probability rises: from 0.3 to roughly 0.32 (more likely next time).
Over many episodes, good actions build up larger advantages, pulling the policy toward them.

matters: Policy gradient is foundational because every intelligent system that learns by trial and error uses it, in some form. In reinforcement learning for robotics, a robot learns to grasp objects by trying grasps, measuring success, and nudging its neural network policy toward successful grasps and away from failures. In LLM training with reinforcement feedback from humans—called RLHF—policy gradient methods like PPO improve the model by making it more likely to generate responses that humans rate as good and less likely to generate ones rated as bad. In alignment and safety research, policy gradient is the mechanism that teaches models to follow human values: you rate an output as aligned or not, compute the advantage, and the policy gradient steers the model away from unaligned behavior. In multi-agent systems and robotics, agents coordinate by each improving their own policy based on the reward signal. Diffusion models also use a variant: instead of discrete actions, they choose directions in high-dimensional space (each direction scored by quality), and policy gradient-like methods steer sampling toward regions that produce higher-quality images.

The core strength is that policy gradient turns a reinforcement learning problem—learn to maximize total reward—into a simple recipe: take the direction that makes good actions more likely, scaled by how good they were. This is why it scales from toy problems to training trillion-parameter language models: the formula is just a few lines of code, but it applies equally to toy Cartpole environments and real-world systems making complex decisions. The logarithm appears because it converts the policy probability into a direction you can follow—if you did an action with low probability and it was good, the gradient of the log tells you how much to nudge the policy to raise that action's probability. Without the logarithm, the math breaks down. The advantage weighting matters because it tells the algorithm not to increase all actions equally, but to put more weight on actions that actually worked. This prevents learning from random noise and aligns every update with actual performance.
